title: The Ozone Layer: Earth's Sunscreen
summary: How a thin layer of gas high above Earth shields us from the sun's harmful rays, and how nations worked together to repair the damage people caused to it.
poll: A big environmental problem, once it starts, can never be fixed.

versions.title: Earth's Sunscreen in the Sky
versions.text:
The sun gives us light. Most of this light is good. But some light is harmful. It can hurt our skin. It can hurt our eyes too. We call it UV light.

High in the sky, there is a thin layer. It is made of gas. It goes around the Earth. We call it the ozone layer. It blocks the harmful rays. It works like a big sunscreen.

Long ago, people used a gas. They used it in old fridges. They used it in spray cans too. This gas rose up high. It broke apart the layer. In the 1980s, people found a big hole. The hole was in the layer. It was over a cold place.

People got worried. Many lands made a plan. They said they would stop the gas. Now the layer is healing. It is slowly getting well. This shows people can fix big problems. They just need to work as one.

People all over got worried. Many lands made a plan. They agreed to stop using that gas. Now the layer is slowly healing. This shows that people can fix even a big problem when they work together.

versions.title: The Ozone Layer
versions.text:
The sun gives us light every day. Most of this light is good for life on Earth. But some light is harmful, and it can hurt our skin and eyes. We call it UV light, or ultraviolet light.

High in the sky, there is a thin layer made of gas. It wraps all around the Earth. It blocks most of the harmful rays from the sun. It works like a big sunscreen for the Earth. We call this layer the ozone layer.

For many years, people used a certain gas. They used it in old fridges and in spray cans. This gas slowly rose up high into the sky, and it broke apart the layer bit by bit. In the 1980s, people found a huge hole in the layer. It was over a cold place far to the south.

People all over the world grew worried. Many lands came together and made a plan. They agreed to stop using the gas that was causing the harm. Now the layer has slowly been getting better.

This story teaches a lesson: when people work together, they can fix even a big problem.

versions.title: The Ozone Layer
versions.text:
The sun gives us light every day, and most of this light supports life on Earth. But some light is harmful, and it can hurt our skin and eyes over time. We call it UV light, or ultraviolet light.

High above the ground, there is a thin layer made of gas. It wraps all the way around our planet. It blocks most of the harmful rays from the sun before they reach us. It works like a big sunscreen for the Earth. We call this layer the ozone layer.

For many years, people used a certain gas in old fridges, air conditioners, and spray cans. This gas slowly rose up high into the sky, and it broke apart tiny bits of the layer. In the 1980s, scientists found a huge hole in the layer. It was over a very cold place far to the south.

People all over the world grew worried when they heard this news. Many lands came together and made a plan. They agreed to stop using the harmful gas that was causing the damage. Since then, the layer has slowly been healing itself.

This story teaches an important lesson: when people work together, they can fix even a very big problem.

versions.title: The Ozone Layer: Earth's Sunscreen
versions.text:
A person can get sunburned in under thirty minutes in strong sun. Yet the sun's rays would be far more dangerous without a thin shield high above us. This shield is the ozone layer. Scientists call it Earth's natural sunscreen.

The ozone layer sits in part of the atmosphere far above the ground. It is made of ozone, a special gas. Ozone forms when three oxygen atoms join together, instead of the usual two. This lets ozone soak up much of the sun's ultraviolet light, often called UV light. Without this shield, too much UV light would reach people, animals, and plants. It could harm skin, hurt eyes, and slow crop growth.

For decades, people did not know that certain man-made chemicals were harming the ozone layer. These chemicals were called CFCs. They were common in fridges, air units, and spray cans. Once released, CFCs drifted upward. They broke apart ozone bit by bit. In 1985, scientists found a huge hole in the ozone layer above Antarctica. The news alarmed people everywhere.

In 1987, almost every country signed a deal called the Montreal Protocol. They agreed to stop making these chemicals. This teamwork worked. Checks today show the ozone layer is slowly getting better. Scientists protect this progress by watching it closely.

The story of the ozone layer offers a lesson. When nations act together, based on good evidence, they can fix harm that once seemed permanent.

versions.title: The Ozone Layer: Earth's Sunscreen
versions.text:
A person can develop a sunburn in under thirty minutes in strong midday sun. Yet the sun's rays would be far more dangerous without a thin shield high above us, one found within the stratosphere. This natural shield makes life as we know it possible on land.

The stratosphere sits above the layer where we breathe and live, and it holds most of Earth's ozone. Ozone is a special molecule formed when three oxygen atoms join together, rather than the two atoms in the air we breathe. This lets ozone absorb much of the sun's ultraviolet radiation before it reaches the ground. Without this shield, too much radiation would reach people, animals, and plants, harming skin, eyes, and crops across whole regions. Long-term exposure to this radiation can raise the risk of skin damage and eye problems in people of any age.

For decades, people did not know that certain man-made chemicals, called CFCs, were destroying ozone molecules in the stratosphere. These chemicals were common in refrigerators, air conditioners, and spray cans. Once released, CFC molecules drifted upward and broke apart ozone through a chain of reactions. In 1985, scientists found a huge hole in the ozone layer above Antarctica, a discovery that drew urgent attention. Researchers tracked the size of the hole using instruments carried on satellites and weather balloons.

In 1987, nearly every country signed a treaty called the Montreal Protocol, agreeing to stop making these chemicals. This remarkable treaty proved successful. Many nations also began developing safer replacement chemicals for refrigeration and cooling systems. Measurements today show the ozone layer is slowly recovering, atom by atom and molecule by molecule.

The story of the ozone layer offers a lesson: when nations act together and sign a treaty based on good evidence, they can repair harm that once seemed permanent.

versions.title: The Ozone Layer: Earth's Sunscreen
versions.text:
High above the surface of the Earth, within a layer of the atmosphere called the stratosphere, lies a thin band of a specialized molecule known as ozone, one that absorbs the majority of the sun's harmful ultraviolet radiation before it can reach the ground. Ozone forms when three oxygen atoms bond together, rather than the two atoms that make up the oxygen we breathe, and this arrangement gives ozone its remarkable ability to intercept radiation that would otherwise damage skin, harm eyes, and reduce the yields of crops across vast agricultural regions.

For much of the twentieth century, manufacturers around the world produced enormous quantities of chemicals called chlorofluorocarbons, or CFCs, prizing them for refrigerators, air conditioners, and aerosol spray cans because they seemed stable, inexpensive, and harmless. No one suspected that these molecules, once released into the air, would drift upward for years until reaching the stratosphere, where sunlight would break them apart and release chlorine atoms capable of destroying thousands of ozone molecules each.

In 1985, researchers studying the atmosphere above Antarctica discovered a startling thinning of the ozone layer, a phenomenon the public soon called the ozone hole. The discovery triggered rapid scientific investigation and, remarkably, swift political action. Within two years, representatives from nearly every country on Earth negotiated and signed the Montreal Protocol, an international treaty committing their nations to phase out CFC production on an agreed schedule.

The treaty's success offers one of the clearest examples in modern history of effective international environmental cooperation. Compliance was high, alternative chemicals were developed quickly, and atmospheric monitoring continued steadily in the following decades. Satellite measurements and ground-based instruments now confirm that ozone concentrations in the stratosphere are slowly increasing again, molecule by molecule, and scientists estimate that the ozone layer could return to its pre-1980 condition sometime around the middle of this century.

This recovery, however, required patience, since CFC molecules can remain active in the atmosphere for many decades after release, meaning the damage done in the twentieth century continued affecting the ozone layer long after the treaty took effect. Scientists therefore continue monitoring atmospheric data closely, aware that new, unregulated chemicals could someday pose a similar threat if left unaddressed.

The story of the ozone layer ultimately demonstrates that environmental problems caused by human activity, however severe, are not necessarily permanent, provided that nations act on solid scientific evidence and sustain their commitment over time rather than abandoning it once initial progress appears.

versions.title: The Ozone Layer: Earth's Sunscreen
versions.text:
High above the surface of the Earth, within a region of the atmosphere known as the stratosphere, lies a thin band of a specialized molecule called ozone, one that absorbs the overwhelming majority of the sun's potentially harmful ultraviolet radiation before that radiation can ever reach the ground below. Ozone forms specifically when three oxygen atoms bond together, rather than the two atoms that typically make up the oxygen molecules we breathe, and this particular atomic arrangement gives ozone its remarkable capacity to intercept radiation that would otherwise damage skin, harm eyes, and substantially reduce the yields of crops across vast agricultural regions throughout the world.

For much of the twentieth century, manufacturers across many countries produced enormous quantities of synthetic chemicals called chlorofluorocarbons, commonly abbreviated as CFCs, prizing them for use in refrigerators, air conditioners, and aerosol spray cans because these chemicals seemed remarkably stable, inexpensive to produce, and entirely harmless to handle. Virtually no one suspected at the time that these seemingly inert molecules, once released into the surrounding air, would gradually drift upward over a period of years until eventually reaching the stratosphere, where intense sunlight would break them apart and release highly reactive chlorine atoms, each one capable of destroying many thousands of ozone molecules through repeated chemical reactions.

In 1985, researchers systematically studying the atmosphere above Antarctica discovered a startling and unexpected thinning of the ozone layer there, a phenomenon the public soon began referring to simply as the ozone hole. This alarming discovery triggered rapid scientific investigation across multiple countries and, remarkably, equally swift and coordinated political action. Within just two years, representatives from nearly every country on Earth successfully negotiated and signed the Montreal Protocol, a binding international treaty committing their respective nations to phase out CFC production entirely according to an agreed and carefully monitored schedule.

The treaty's ultimate success offers one of the clearest and most frequently cited examples in modern history of genuinely effective international environmental cooperation. Compliance among signatory nations proved consistently high, viable alternative chemicals were developed and adopted quickly by industry, and careful atmospheric monitoring continued steadily throughout the following decades without significant interruption. Satellite measurements combined with ground-based instruments now confirm that ozone concentrations within the stratosphere are slowly but measurably increasing once again, essentially molecule by molecule, and atmospheric scientists currently estimate that the ozone layer could plausibly return to something resembling its pre-1980 condition sometime around the middle of this century.

This gradual recovery, however, required considerable patience from scientists and policymakers alike, since individual CFC molecules can remain chemically active within the atmosphere for many decades after their initial release, meaning that damage inflicted during the twentieth century continued measurably affecting the ozone layer long after the treaty itself first took effect. Atmospheric scientists therefore continue monitoring relevant data closely even today, keenly aware that new and currently unregulated chemicals could potentially someday pose a strikingly similar threat if such substances were ever left unaddressed by future international agreements.

The story of the ozone layer ultimately demonstrates, perhaps more clearly than almost any other environmental case, that problems caused by human activity, however severe or seemingly irreversible they initially appear, are not necessarily permanent, provided that nations are willing to act decisively on solid scientific evidence and are able to sustain their shared commitment over time rather than abandoning that commitment once early signs of progress first begin to appear.

wrong.D: Recovery shows the agreement did have a real effect.

questions.stem: How does the author mainly organize the article?
options: By telling a made-up story about a scientist
By listing the ingredients needed to make sunscreen
By explaining the problem, its cause, and the solution
By comparing life in Antarctica to life in the desert
questions.why: The article first explains the ozone layer's purpose, then the damage caused by CFCs, and finally the global solution.

wrong.A: The article is nonfiction, not a made-up story.
wrong.B: The article does not describe how to make sunscreen.
wrong.D: The article does not compare Antarctica to the desert.

MID.prompt: Explain what caused the hole in the ozone layer and how countries worked together to fix it. Use at least two key words from the article.
checklist: I explained the cause of the ozone hole.
I used at least two key words correctly.
MID.modelAnswer: The hole in the ozone layer was caused by CFCs, man-made chemicals that drifted into the atmosphere and broke apart ozone molecules, reducing the protection ozone gives against ultraviolet radiation. In 1987, nearly every country signed the Montreal Protocol, agreeing to stop producing these harmful chemicals, and since then the ozone layer has slowly started to protect us the way it once did.

keyWords.definition: the layer of Earth's atmosphere above the one we breathe in, where most ozone is found
keyWords.example: Some weather balloons rise high enough to reach the stratosphere.

keyWords.definition: a group of atoms joined together, the smallest unit of a substance that keeps its properties
keyWords.example: A molecule of water is made of two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.

keyWords.definition: energy that travels through space as waves or rays
keyWords.example: Doctors use careful amounts of radiation to take X-ray pictures.

keyWords.definition: a formal written agreement between countries
keyWords.example: The two nations signed a treaty to share the river's water fairly.

keyWords.definition: an extremely small particle that is a basic building block of matter
keyWords.example: Every substance in the universe is made of tiny atoms.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the article?
options: The Montreal Protocol was signed only by a few nations in Europe, so it had no effect on the sky
The stratosphere contains no ozone at all, so there is nothing for people to repair
International cooperation based on evidence can repair severe damage to the ozone layer
CFCs are no longer dangerous once they reach the stratosphere, and they help the ozone layer
questions.why: The article shows how global cooperation, guided by scientific evidence, repaired serious damage to the ozone layer.

wrong.A: Nearly every country in the world signed the treaty, not just a few in Europe.
wrong.B: The stratosphere holds most of Earth's ozone.
wrong.D: CFCs remain dangerous after reaching the stratosphere, where they destroy ozone.

questions.stem: Where is most of Earth's ozone located?
options: In the stratosphere
Deep underground
Only above the equator
In the layer of air we breathe
questions.why: The article states that the stratosphere contains the vast majority of Earth's ozone.

wrong.B: Ozone is found in the atmosphere, not underground.
wrong.C: The article does not limit ozone to the equator.
wrong.D: The layer we breathe is below the stratosphere, where ozone is concentrated.

questions.stem: According to the article, what happens when a chlorine atom from a broken-down CFC molecule reacts with ozone?
options: It instantly cools the stratosphere around the Earth
It turns into a new treaty between nations
It creates more oxygen atoms for the air
It can destroy thousands of ozone molecules
questions.why: Each chlorine atom can destroy thousands of ozone molecules.

wrong.A: The article does not describe chlorine cooling the stratosphere.
wrong.B: Treaties are agreements made by people, not chemical reactions.
wrong.C: Chlorine breaks ozone apart; it does not create new oxygen atoms.

questions.stem: The article explains that ozone forms from three oxygen atoms bonding together. What does atom mean here?
options: A kind of international treaty between nations that protects air
A tiny particle that is a basic building block of matter
A type of harmful man-made chemical compound that is made in labs
A measurement unit used for radiation levels in the sky
questions.why: In the article, atoms are the tiny particles that join together to form molecules like ozone.

wrong.A: A treaty is an agreement, not a particle.
wrong.C: An atom is not itself a chemical compound.
wrong.D: An atom is a particle, not a unit of measurement.

questions.stem: Why did CFC molecules end up damaging ozone in the stratosphere?
options: They drifted upward, broke apart, and released chlorine
They reacted chemically with treaties signed back in 1987
They were banned by governments many years too early
They absorbed too much radiation themselves
questions.why: The article explains that CFC molecules slowly rose into the stratosphere, where sunlight broke them apart and released chlorine that destroyed ozone.

wrong.B: Treaties are legal agreements and do not chemically react with molecules.
wrong.C: The article says CFCs caused damage for decades before being banned, not that the ban was too early.
wrong.D: The article describes ozone, not CFCs, as absorbing radiation.

questions.stem: CFC molecules can stay active in the atmosphere for decades. What can you infer about the ozone layer's recovery?
options: It would happen within a single year of banning CFCs, because the gas disappears quickly
It has nothing to do with how long CFCs remain active in the air above us
It depends only on how much ozone existed before 1980, not on any chemicals
It naturally takes a long time, even after the harmful chemical is banned
questions.why: Since CFC molecules remain active for decades, their damaging effects continue long after they are banned, so recovery is naturally slow.

wrong.A: The article says recovery is expected to take until the middle of this century, not one year.
wrong.B: How long CFCs remain active directly affects how long recovery takes.
wrong.C: The article connects recovery time to how long CFCs stay active, not just past ozone levels.

questions.stem: Why might scientists worry about new, unregulated chemicals in the future?
options: Because any new chemical automatically becomes a treaty
Because the Montreal Protocol already prevents all possible future chemicals
Because such chemicals could potentially damage the ozone layer the way CFCs once did
Because new chemicals always strengthen the stratosphere
questions.why: Scientists stay alert because new chemicals could harm the ozone layer the way CFCs did.

wrong.A: A chemical is not the same thing as a treaty.
wrong.B: The Montreal Protocol addressed known chemicals at the time, not every possible future one.
wrong.D: The article warns new chemicals could harm, not strengthen, the stratosphere.

questions.stem: Why does the author describe both the scientific discovery of the ozone hole and the political response to it?
options: To argue that governments never act quickly during an environmental crisis
To show how evidence and cooperation solved a global problem
To compare Antarctica with other continents
To criticize scientists for raising unnecessary concerns
questions.why: Describing both the discovery and the treaty shows readers how science and cooperation combined to solve a serious problem.

wrong.A: The article shows governments acting quickly, within just two years.
wrong.C: The article does not compare continents.
wrong.D: The article praises the scientific discovery rather than criticizing it.

HIGH.prompt: Explain how scientific evidence and international cooperation worked together to address damage to the ozone layer. Support your explanation with evidence from the article.
checklist: I explained the role of international cooperation.
I supported my explanation with evidence from the article.
HIGH.modelAnswer: Scientists first provided the evidence by discovering, in 1985, an enormous hole in the ozone layer above Antarctica caused by CFC molecules releasing chlorine atoms that destroyed ozone in the stratosphere. International cooperation followed quickly, as nearly every country signed the Montreal Protocol treaty in 1987, agreeing to stop producing CFCs. Together, this scientific evidence and global agreement allowed the ozone layer to begin recovering, showing how nations can repair serious environmental radiation damage when they act on reliable research.

LOW.stem: What can harmful UV light hurt?
options: Our hair and teeth
Our skin and eyes
Our shoes and bags
Our hands and feet
LOW.why: In the text, UV light can hurt our skin and our eyes.

wrong.A: The text does not say UV light hurts hair or teeth.
wrong.C: Shoes and bags are not mentioned.
wrong.D: The text names skin and eyes, not hands and feet.

LOW.stem: What does the author mean by "It works like a big sunscreen"?
options: It makes the sky look blue
It makes the sun look bright
It makes the air feel cool
It keeps harmful light away
LOW.why: The ozone layer blocks the harmful rays, as a sunscreen protects skin.

wrong.A: The text does not talk about the color of the sky.
wrong.B: The layer blocks harmful rays and does not make the sun brighter.
wrong.C: The text does not say the layer cools the air.

LOW.stem: Where did people use the old gas long ago?
options: In fridges and spray cans
In cars and city buses
In shoes and school bags
In pens and paper books
LOW.why: In the text, people used the gas in old fridges and spray cans.

wrong.B: Cars and buses are not mentioned.
wrong.C: Shoes and bags are not mentioned.
wrong.D: Pens and books are not mentioned.

LOW.stem: Why did people get worried in the 1980s?
options: The sun was getting colder
The old fridges stopped working
They found a hole in the layer
The spray cans ran out of gas
LOW.why: The text says people found a big hole in the ozone layer in the 1980s and then got worried.

wrong.A: The text does not say the sun got colder.
wrong.B: The fridges are mentioned only because their gas harmed the layer.
wrong.D: The text does not say the cans ran out of gas.

MID.stem: About how fast can a person get sunburned in strong sun?
options: In about two long days
In about one whole week
In about two full hours
In under thirty minutes
MID.why: In the text, a person can get sunburned in under thirty minutes in strong sun.

wrong.A: Two days is far too long.
wrong.B: A week is far too long.
wrong.C: Two hours is longer than the text says.

MID.stem: The article says nations fixed harm that once seemed permanent. What does permanent mean?
options: lasting forever
very small
easy to see
quick to fix
MID.why: The harm to the ozone layer seemed like it would last forever, but nations acted to fix it.

wrong.B: The harm was large, not small.
wrong.C: The word is not about seeing.
wrong.D: Quick to fix is the opposite of permanent.

MID.stem: Why did people use CFCs for many years?
options: They wanted a bigger hole
They had no other fridges
They did not know the harm
A treaty told them to
MID.why: The text says people did not know that CFCs were harming the ozone layer.

wrong.A: No one wanted to make a hole.
wrong.B: The text does not say there were no other fridges.
wrong.D: The treaty told them to stop making CFCs.

MID.stem: Why does the author end with a lesson about nations acting together?
options: To say the hole is bigger today
To show teamwork can fix harm
To explain how ozone is made
To list the uses of spray cans
MID.why: The ending says that when nations act together on good evidence, they can fix harm that seemed permanent.

wrong.A: The ozone layer is slowly getting better.
wrong.C: How ozone forms is explained earlier.
wrong.D: Spray cans are only mentioned as one use of CFCs.

HIGH.stem: How did researchers track the size of the ozone hole?
options: By measuring shadows at midday
By counting sunburned beachgoers
By using satellites and tools
By testing the water in the sea
HIGH.why: Researchers used satellites and other instruments to measure the ozone layer.

wrong.A: Shadows are not mentioned.
wrong.B: The text does not say they counted sunburned people.
wrong.D: The sea is not mentioned.

HIGH.stem: In 1987, nearly every country signed a treaty. What is a treaty?
options: a kind of chemical
a tool for measuring the air
an agreement between nations
a layer of the sky
HIGH.why: Countries signed the Montreal Protocol, agreeing to stop making the harmful chemicals, so a treaty is an agreement between nations.

wrong.A: The chemicals are what the treaty stopped.
wrong.B: Instruments measure the air, not treaties.
wrong.D: The stratosphere is a layer; a treaty is not.

HIGH.stem: What did measurements show after nearly every country agreed to stop making CFCs?
options: The ozone layer is slowly recovering
The ozone hole quickly doubled in size
No change happened anywhere at all
The stratosphere disappeared entirely
HIGH.why: The text says the treaty proved successful and measurements show the ozone layer is slowly recovering.

wrong.B: The text says the layer is recovering, not getting worse.
wrong.C: The text says the layer is recovering, so there was a change.
wrong.D: The stratosphere did not disappear.

HIGH.stem: The article says the ozone layer is only slowly recovering. What does this suggest about the repair?
options: It was finished in one year
It takes a long time to heal
It can never be repaired
It needs no more care
HIGH.why: Even after the chemicals were stopped, the ozone layer recovers only slowly, so the repair takes a long time.

wrong.A: Slow recovery means it was not finished quickly.
wrong.C: The layer is recovering, so it can be repaired.
wrong.D: Slow recovery shows care and patience are still needed.
